book.title: Linear Algebra
book.subtitle: From systems to spaces, projections, and factorizations
book.author: AI University · AI-generated
book.description: A complete finite-dimensional introduction: systems, matrices and maps, vector spaces, the four fundamental subspaces, determinants, eigenvalues, orthogonality, least squares, symmetric matrices, SVD, networks, and data applications.
book.audience: For readers with elementary algebra and plane geometry; rotations use basic trigonometry, with no calculus prerequisite
book.scope: Ten chapters and fifty lessons form a complete introductory course in finite-dimensional real vector spaces and matrices, including complex eigenvalues, pseudoinverses, low-rank approximation, conditioning, and PCA. Full Jordan theory, abstract duality, tensors, and infinite-dimensional analysis are left to later volumes.

glossary.meaning: A linear combination scales and adds fixed vectors to form a new vector.

glossary.term: Row and column views of a system
glossary.meaning: A system describes both an intersection of geometric constraints and a linear combination.
Elimination removes unknowns step by step while preserving the entire solution set.
Pivots identify independent constraints on variables. A contradiction row signals no solution.

glossary.term: Parametric form and the full solution set
glossary.meaning: A particular solution plus every homogeneous solution describes all solutions of a consistent linear system.
A matrix-vector product combines the matrix columns using the input coefficients.
A linear map preserves addition and scalar multiplication, so its basis images determine it completely.
Matrices for composed maps multiply in right-to-left order of action.

glossary.term: Inverses and the invertible matrix theorem
glossary.meaning: An invertible square matrix allows each output to recover exactly one input.
LU saves elimination steps so one coefficient matrix can handle multiple right-hand sides.
A subspace is a subset that remains closed under the original addition and scalar multiplication.
The span is the set of all linear combinations of the given vectors.
Independence means that only all-zero coefficients combine the vectors to give zero.
A basis spans the entire space without redundancy, giving unique coordinates.
Every basis of a finite-dimensional space has the same size, called its dimension.

glossary.term: Basis coordinates and change of basis
glossary.meaning: A change of basis changes a vector's coordinates, not the vector itself.
The null space contains all input directions that the matrix sends to zero.
The column space contains reachable outputs. The row space is spanned by the rows viewed as vectors in the input space.
Input dimension equals the dimension of independent outputs plus the dimension lost completely.
The rows, columns, and two kernels split input and output into complementary orthogonal parts.
The determinant's magnitude gives volume scaling; its sign records an orientation reversal.
Row-operation and product rules let you calculate determinants during elimination.
Expanding along one row or column recursively reduces a determinant's size.
A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Cramer's rule expresses the unique solution using determinants of replaced columns.
An eigenvector is a nonzero vector whose image is a scalar multiple of itself.
The characteristic polynomial finds all scalar shifts that make a matrix singular.
A repeated eigenvalue need not provide enough independent eigenvectors.
In an eigenvector basis, the matrix is diagonal and scales each coordinate separately.
A real matrix may lack real eigendirections. Complex numbers extend eigenvalue language to rotation.
The inner product measures alignment and defines length and distance.
Orthogonal projection is the vector in a specified subspace nearest to the target.
The orthogonal complement contains vectors perpendicular to every vector in a subspace.
Orthogonalization removes projections onto known directions, retaining each new independent part.
QR expresses matrix columns using orthonormal directions and their combination coefficients.
When an exact system has no solution, least squares minimizes squared residual length.

glossary.term: Real symmetric matrices and the spectral theorem
glossary.meaning: Every real symmetric matrix is diagonalizable in an orthonormal eigenbasis.
A real symmetric quadratic form becomes a signed sum of squares in an orthonormal basis.
Positive definiteness requires a strictly positive quadratic form for every nonzero input.
A real symmetric positive definite matrix uniquely factors into a lower-triangular matrix with positive diagonal times its transpose.

glossary.term: Rayleigh quotients and extrema on the unit sphere
glossary.meaning: A symmetric matrix's quadratic-form extrema on the unit sphere are its smallest and largest eigenvalues.
Singular values measure length scaling along special orthogonal input directions and are always nonnegative.
Every real matrix factors into an orthogonal input transformation, nonnegative directional scaling, and an orthogonal output transformation.
The pseudoinverse selects the shortest input among all least-squares solutions.

glossary.term: Truncated SVD and optimal low-rank approximation
glossary.meaning: Keeping the largest singular values approximates a matrix with fewer directions and gives exact truncation errors.
A condition number bounds how small data errors can amplify into relative solution errors in sensitive directions.
A Markov matrix updates a distribution with nonnegative transition probabilities. A steady state is a probability vector with eigenvalue one.
A linear recurrence repeatedly applies one matrix. Eigendirections determine how components grow, decay, or oscillate.

glossary.term: Graphs, incidence matrices, and flow conservation
glossary.meaning: An incidence matrix converts directed edge flows into net inflows at nodes.
PCA finds orthogonal directions retaining the most variance in centered data.
Decide whether you need an exact solve, an approximate fit, repeated iteration, or compression before choosing a factorization.

appendices.title: Vector space axioms
appendices.text: Over the real numbers, a vector set has addition and scalar multiplication. Addition is closed, commutative, and associative, with zero and additive inverses. Scaling is closed and satisfies $a(u+v)=au+av$, $(a+b)v=av+bv$, $a(bv)=(ab)v$, and $1v=v$. Together these define a real vector space. Matrices and bounded-degree polynomials use ordinary operations, satisfying the rules componentwise or coefficientwise. Different operations must be checked anew; an object's name does not settle the axioms.

appendices.title: Notation, matrix norms, and complex conventions
appendices.text: Vectors are columns; $A^T$ denotes transpose and $A^*=\bar A^T$ conjugate transpose. The standard real inner product is $x^Ty$. Our complex convention is $x^*y$, conjugate-linear in the first argument. Matrix two-norm is $\max_{\|x\|=1}\|Ax\|$ and Frobenius norm $\|A\|_F=(\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}$. A maximum over unit vectors exists because a continuous function on a finite-dimensional compact set attains its extrema. This basic analytical fact does not require completing a computational calculus course first.

appendices.title: Why the exchange lemma makes dimension unique
appendices.text: Suppose $u_1,\ldots,u_k$ is independent and $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ spans the space. Express $u_1$ in that spanning list; some coefficient is nonzero, allowing replacement of the corresponding $v_j$ by $u_1$ without losing the span. At $u_2$, representation using only the already inserted $u_1$ would violate independence, so another original vector can be replaced. Repeating for the independent list requires $k\le m$. Applying this in both directions to two bases gives equal sizes and also yields finite-dimensional extension and reduction results.

appendices.title: Why row rank, column rank, and nullity count pivots
appendices.text: Reversible row operations preserve the row space, homogeneous solutions, and column-dependence coefficients. Distinct leading positions make nonzero echelon rows independent. Pivot columns are independent and generate all other columns; invertible row operations transfer these relations back to the original matrix. Thus row and column ranks both count pivots. Setting one free variable to one and the others to zero gives independent homogeneous special solutions, whose parameter form spans the kernel. Rank plus nullity therefore equals the column count.

appendices.title: Determinants and volume: definition and scope
appendices.text: A determinant is uniquely determined by multilinearity in columns, sign reversal under column swaps, and value one on the identity. Expanding columns in the standard basis leaves only terms selecting each row and column once, producing the signed permutation sum. Repeated columns give zero; shear invariance, scale factors, and swap signs follow. An invertible map factors into elementary transformations, whose volume factors multiply to the absolute determinant. A singular map has a lower-dimensional image and zero volume in the original dimension.

appendices.title: Outline of the real symmetric spectral theorem
appendices.text: Maximize $x^TAx$ on the unit sphere at $v$. For any unit $w$ perpendicular to $v$, examine $q(v\cos t+w\sin t)$. If $v^TAw\ne0$, a sufficiently small $t$ of the same sign makes the linear change dominate quadratic terms, contradicting maximality. Thus $Av$ is parallel to $v$. Symmetry makes $v^\perp$ invariant under $A$: $v^TAw=(Av)^Tw=0$. Restrict to this lower-dimensional orthogonal complement and induct to obtain a complete orthonormal eigenbasis.

appendices.title: Multiplicity bounds and minimum-norm solutions
appendices.text: Extend a basis of an eigenspace to the whole space. In this basis the matrix has upper-left block $\lambda I_g$ and zero lower-left block, so its characteristic polynomial contains at least factor $(t-\lambda)^g$. Geometric multiplicity cannot exceed algebraic multiplicity. For minimum norm, all least-squares inputs differ by kernel vectors. The pseudoinverse solution lies in the row space, perpendicular to the kernel, so adding kernel components only increases squared length.

appendices.title: Frobenius optimality of low-rank approximation
appendices.text: For any rank-at-most-$k$ approximation $B$, place its column space inside a space $W$ of dimension at most $k$, with orthogonal projection $P$. Columnwise nearest-point optimality gives $\|A-B\|_F^2\ge\|(I-P)A\|_F^2=\|A\|_F^2-\|PA\|_F^2$. In the left singular basis, the retained part is $\sum_i\sigma_i^2\|Pu_i\|^2$. These weights lie between zero and one and sum to at most $k$, so this is bounded by the sum of the largest $k$ squared singular values. Taking the first $k$ left singular directions attains the bound.

appendices.title: Markov convergence and the limits of this volume
appendices.text: Perron-Frobenius theory gives a unique steady state for a finite strictly positive column-stochastic matrix, with all other eigenvalues of magnitude below one. We cite rather than fully prove it. Nonnegative matrices not strictly positive need separate irreducibility and aperiodicity checks; finite animation does not establish convergence. Full Jordan form, abstract duality, tensors, general fields, infinite-dimensional operators, FFT, and systematic linear-programming algorithms belong to later volumes. This volume completes an introductory course in finite-dimensional real matrices and vector spaces.

appendices.title: Finite diagrams and numerical precision
appendices.text: Geometry uses finite grids and floating-point numbers. Nearly dependent and exactly dependent vectors have different ranks. Intersections or inverse images can lie far outside the viewport; when omitted, their status must still be explained. Numerical tests check specific examples and models, not general theorems. Treating a small singular value as zero is a numerical modeling decision; these exact examples and diagrams do not silently replace arbitrary small nonzero values by zero.

body.title: What does a vector record?
body.text: A vector in $\mathbb R^n$ has $n$ real components. Add only vectors of the same dimension, component by component. This book uses column vectors.

body.title: What do coefficients control?
body.text: In $a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v$, scale each direction by a signed coefficient, then add. Negative coefficients reverse direction; zero leaves a vector out.

body.title: How do you check a representation?
body.text: Check each component. Looking close in a diagram does not establish equality. A vector may have several linear-combination representations.

conditions: All vectors belong to the same real coordinate space; coefficients are real.

derivation.text: Scale each component.
Then add.
Compare corresponding components.

body.title: What makes an equation linear?
body.text: Unknowns appear only to the first power, with known coefficients. Neither $xy=1$ nor $x^2+y=0$ is linear.

body.title: What does the row view show?
body.text: A nondegenerate equation in two variables describes a line. Common points solve the system. Distinct parallel lines have no solution; coincident lines share every point. A degenerate equation may describe the whole plane or the empty set.

body.title: How does the column view match?
body.text: Treat unknowns as coefficients of column vectors. In $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$, their linear combination equals the right-hand side.

lessons.subtitle: Rewrite constraints without changing solutions
lessons.concept: Elimination removes unknowns step by step while preserving the entire solution set.
lessons.intuition: Subtracting a multiple of one row from another rewrites a constraint using known information. The operation is reversible, so no solution is lost.
objectives: Apply row operations to an augmented matrix
Solve by back substitution

body.title: Which row operations are valid?
body.text: Swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero scalar, or add a multiple of another row. Each is reversible.

body.title: How do you use an augmented matrix?
body.text: Write coefficients and the right-hand side together as $[A\mid\mathbf b]$. Apply each operation to the whole row, including the right-hand side.

body.title: When do you back substitute?
body.text: After reaching echelon form, solve upward from the last nonzero equation. Continue clearing above pivots and scaling them to one to obtain reduced echelon form.

conditions: A row scale factor must be nonzero. Row operations preserve solutions but generally change the matrix as a linear map.

derivation.text: Choose a nonzero pivot.
Eliminate the entries below it.
Back substitute or continue eliminating.

workedExamples.title: Solve in two steps
steps: Subtract twice the first equation from the second to get $y=2$.
Substitute into the first equation to get $x=1$.

workedExamples.title: A row swap is needed
steps: Swap rows to place a nonzero pivot in the first column.
workedExamples.answer: $(1,2)$. A zero first coefficient does not imply inconsistency.

commonMistakes.claim: Multiplying an entire row by zero preserves solutions.
commonMistakes.correction: It discards an original constraint.

commonMistakes.claim: The right-hand side is excluded from elimination.
commonMistakes.correction: Both sides must change together.

What reverses $R_2\leftarrow R_2-3R_1$?
practice.hint: Add back the quantity that was subtracted.

practice.hint: Back substitute from bottom to top.

solution: A column swap reorders variables; record the label change too.

choices: Multiply an entire row by zero
learningCheck.explanation: Multiplication by zero turns a constraint into an identity.

teaching.explain: Elimination rewrites the same constraints in an easier form. Each step should be reversible.

lessons.title: Pivots, consistency, and free variables
lessons.subtitle: Check contradictions before counting free variables
lessons.concept: Pivots identify independent constraints on variables. A contradiction row signals no solution.
lessons.intuition: Some equations repeat earlier constraints. Nonzero rows left after elimination reveal how many independent constraints remain.
objectives: Identify pivots and contradiction rows
Classify systems using consistency and free variables

body.title: Where are the pivots?
body.text: In echelon form, each nonzero row begins with a pivot. Successive pivots lie strictly farther right; zero rows appear at the bottom.

body.title: How do you recognize inconsistency?
body.text: An augmented row $[0\ \cdots\ 0\mid d]$ with $d\ne0$ states $0=d$, so no solution exists.

body.title: How do you classify a consistent system?
body.text: Without contradiction rows, nonpivot columns correspond to free variables. No free variables gives one solution; at least one gives infinitely many real solutions.

conditions: Rank counts pivots in echelon form. Count only coefficient columns when identifying free variables.

derivation.text: The coefficient pivot count is the rank.
Each nonpivot unknown can be chosen freely.
First check whether the augmented column adds a pivot.

workedExamples.title: A free variable
steps: Coefficient pivots lie in columns one and three; the second unknown is free.
There is no contradiction row and one free variable.

workedExamples.title: More equations can still be consistent
workedExamples.problem: Does $x=1,y=2,x+y=3$ have too many constraints to be consistent?
steps: The third equation is the sum of the first two.
Elimination produces a zero row rather than a contradiction.

commonMistakes.claim: A zero row means no solution.
commonMistakes.correction: $0=0$ is redundant; $0=d\ne0$ is contradictory.

commonMistakes.claim: The augmented column represents another unknown.
commonMistakes.correction: It records the right-hand side, rather than a variable coefficient.

practice.problem: A consistent system has $3$ unknowns and coefficient rank $2$. How many free variables remain?
What does $[0\ 0\mid 5]$ mean?
practice.hint: Read the row as an equation.

practice.problem: Can $4$ equations in $2$ unknowns have a unique solution?
Can the homogeneous system $A\mathbf x=0$ produce a contradiction row?
practice.hint: The zero vector is always a solution.
solution: A zero right-hand side remains zero after row operations.

interactiveVisual.caption: The constraints are $x+y=2$ and $x+cy=b$. For a singular matrix, distinguish coincident lines from distinct parallel lines.
interactiveVisual.prediction: After changing the right-hand side, must coefficient rank and the existence of a solution change together?

learningCheck.question: How many real solutions does a consistent system with a free variable have?
learningCheck.explanation: A free variable ranges continuously over real values.

teaching.explain: First check for conflicting constraints, then count what remains free. The number of equations alone answers neither question.

steps.title: One intersection
steps.observation: The solution is $(1,1)$; the determinant is one.

steps.title: Repeated constraints
steps.observation: The lines coincide. The coefficient rank is one, with infinitely many solutions.

steps.title: Conflicting constraints
steps.observation: Distinct parallel lines never meet. The augmented rank exceeds the coefficient rank.

lessons.title: Parametric form and the full solution set
lessons.subtitle: A particular solution locates the set; homogeneous solutions give directions
lessons.concept: A particular solution plus every homogeneous solution describes all solutions of a consistent linear system.
lessons.intuition: Two solutions share a right-hand side. Subtracting cancels it, so their difference belongs to the homogeneous solution set.
objectives: Describe every solution with free parameters
Distinguish a linear subspace from an affine solution set

body.title: Where do parameters come from?
body.text: Give each free variable a parameter and express pivot variables in those parameters. Do not add restrictions absent from the equations.

body.title: Why split the solution into two parts?
body.text: Fix a particular solution $\mathbf x_p$ and add any homogeneous solution $\mathbf z$. The identity $A\mathbf z=0$ preserves the right-hand side.

body.title: Must the set contain the origin?
body.text: Homogeneous solution sets contain the origin. A consistent nonhomogeneous set is generally a translate, called an affine set.

formalDefinition.text: Parametric form and the full solution set
conditions: A particular solution must exist. Do not invent one for an inconsistent system. Parameters range over all real numbers.
Here $\ker A=\{z:Az=0\}$ is the homogeneous solution set.

derivation.text: Subtract any two solutions.
Conversely, add a homogeneous solution.
This proves every solution is included.

workedExamples.title: Two free variables
steps: From $x=3-2s+t$, collect the constant and parameter terms.

commonMistakes.claim: Finding one solution finishes the problem.
commonMistakes.correction: Identify and describe every free variable.

commonMistakes.claim: A nonhomogeneous solution set is always a subspace.
commonMistakes.correction: A nonzero right-hand side generally excludes the origin.

practice.problem: How do you write all solutions of $x+y=4$?
Does the solution set of $x-y=0$ contain the origin?
If $A x_1=A x_2=b$, what is $A(x_1-x_2)$?
Is the sum of two solutions of $x+y=1$ also a solution?

interactiveVisual.prediction: Why does moving in a homogeneous direction preserve the right-hand side?

learningCheck.question: What must you add to a particular solution to obtain every solution?
learningCheck.explanation: Only homogeneous directions leave the right-hand side unchanged.

teaching.explain: A particular solution places the line or plane; homogeneous solutions give directions along which movement preserves the constraints.

steps.observation: This gives the particular solution $(1,1,0)$.

lessons.title: Matrices, transposes, and multiplication
lessons.subtitle: Combine columns; calculate by rows
lessons.concept: A matrix-vector product combines the matrix columns using the input coefficients.
lessons.intuition: Count input and output components first. Multiplication is undefined when dimensions do not match.
objectives: Check dimensions
Calculate products and transposes

body.title: What do matrix dimensions mean?
body.text: An $m\times n$ matrix takes $n$ numbers in and produces $m$ numbers. Matrix addition requires matching dimensions; transposition swaps rows and columns.

body.title: How do matrices multiply?
body.text: Column $j$ of $AB$ is $A$ times column $j$ of $B$. Entrywise, take the sum of products of a left row and a right column.

body.title: Does order matter?
body.text: Usually $AB\ne BA$; sometimes only one order is defined. Transposition reverses the order of a product.

conditions: If $A$ is $m\times n$, $B$ must have $n$ rows. The output row count comes from $A$ and column count from $B$.

derivation.text: View the right matrix as columns.
Apply the left matrix to each column.
Expand by components.

commonMistakes.claim: Matrix multiplication multiplies matching entries.
commonMistakes.correction: That defines a different operation, not matrix multiplication here.

commonMistakes.claim: $(AB)^T=A^TB^T$.
commonMistakes.correction: Transposition must reverse the order.

practice.problem: What size results from multiplying an $2\times3$ matrix by an $3\times4$ matrix?
practice.hint: Match the inner dimensions and retain the outer ones.
solution: The inner $3$ matches; the result is $2\times4$.

practice.problem: Given $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$, find $(A^T)_{12}$.
Given $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$, find $A^2$.
Does $AB=0$ imply $A=0$ or $B=0$?
solution: Both $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,0),B=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ are nonzero, but their product is zero.

interactiveVisual.caption: Blue shows the original grid and unit circle; green shows their image under $A$. Gold shows the image of $(1,1)$. The four inputs change the matrix entries.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Which two columns give the images of the unit square's edges?

learningCheck.question: If $A$ is $3\times2$, how many components does the input have?
learningCheck.explanation: Input length equals the column count.

teaching.explain: Each column tells you where one input basis direction goes. Multiplication adds these contributions.

steps.observation: The grid, circle, and vector stay unchanged.

lessons.title: Linear maps and standard matrices
lessons.subtitle: Basis images determine the whole map
lessons.concept: A linear map preserves addition and scalar multiplication, so its basis images determine it completely.
lessons.intuition: Knowing where the two basis directions go determines every vector's image in the plane.
objectives: Check preservation of addition and scaling
Build a matrix from basis images

body.title: How do you test linearity?
body.text: Check $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)$ and $T(cu)=cT(u)$ for all vectors and scalars. Testing a few points does not prove a general map linear.

body.title: How do you find the standard matrix?
body.text: Compute the images of standard basis vectors $e_j$ and put them in columns. A nonzero translation is not linear because it moves the origin.

body.title: Does linear mean a straight line?
body.text: Coordinates, matrices, and polynomials can form vector spaces. Linearity describes operations; it does not require a graph to be a line in one variable.

conditions: The domain and codomain must be vector spaces. We begin with real coordinate spaces.

derivation.text: Express any input in the basis.
Separate terms using linearity.
These images become matrix columns.

workedExamples.title: From a rule to a matrix
steps: Put the two images in columns, in order.

workedExamples.title: Rule out translation
steps: A linear map sends the zero vector to zero.

commonMistakes.claim: Preserving the origin guarantees linearity.
commonMistakes.correction: $T(x)=x^2$ preserves the origin but not addition.

commonMistakes.claim: Standard matrix rows are the basis images.
commonMistakes.correction: Put the images in columns.

practice.problem: Given $T(x,y)=(2x-y,y)$, find $T(0,1)$.
Is $T(x)=|x|$ linear?
practice.hint: Test multiplication by a negative scalar.

practice.problem: Is the zero map linear?
solution: Both sides of each rule are zero.

practice.hint: Combine basis images with the input coefficients.

interactiveVisual.caption: Blue shows the original grid and unit circle; green shows their image under $A$. Gold shows the image of $(1,1)$. The four inputs change the matrix entries.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Which basis image changes when you change one matrix column?

learningCheck.question: Which condition alone rules out linearity?
learningCheck.explanation: Linearity forces zero to map to zero.

teaching.explain: Linear maps can scale, rotate, shear, or collapse directions, but must treat every linear combination consistently.

steps.title: Identity
steps.observation: The grid, circle, and vector stay unchanged.

steps.title: Shear
steps.observation: The unit square tilts while its area remains one.

steps.title: Collapse to a line
steps.observation: Vertical information is lost; rank drops to one.

lessons.title: Composition, rotations, and shears
lessons.subtitle: Apply transformations from right to left
lessons.concept: Matrices for composed maps multiply in right-to-left order of action.
lessons.intuition: Shearing then stretching generally reaches a different point from stretching then shearing.
objectives: Calculate a composite matrix
Explain the order of rotations, reflections, and shears

body.title: Why read a product backward?
body.text: In $(AB)x=A(Bx)$, the rightmost matrix reaches the input first. Write the intermediate vector to keep the order clear.

body.title: How do you represent rotation?
body.text: Rotate both standard basis vectors through the same angle to obtain the matrix columns. Angles are in radians; positive rotation is counterclockwise.

body.title: How do linear and affine maps differ?
body.text: An affine map $Ax+b$ can translate. If $b\ne0$, it is not linear in the original space. Homogeneous coordinates can encode it in a larger matrix without making the original map linear.

conditions: Input and output dimensions must match for composition. Multiplication is associative but generally not commutative.

derivation.text: Apply the right map first.
Then apply the left map.
Combine them into one matrix.

workedExamples.title: Order changes the result
workedExamples.problem: First shear $(0,1)$ by $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, then stretch by $D=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$.
workedExamples.answer: The order is $DS$; the result is $(2,1)$.

workedExamples.title: Two rotations
workedExamples.problem: Where does $(2,1)$ go after two counterclockwise rotations of $\pi/2$?
steps: The second gives $(-2,-1)$, equivalent to rotation through $\pi$.

commonMistakes.claim: $AB$ means apply $A$ first.
commonMistakes.correction: With column vectors, the right matrix acts first.

commonMistakes.claim: Every area-preserving map is a rotation.
commonMistakes.correction: A shear can preserve area while changing angles.

practice.problem: What matrix rotates counterclockwise through $\pi/2$?
What matrix reflects across the horizontal axis?
practice.hint: Keep the horizontal coordinate and negate the vertical one.

practice.problem: What is $R_\theta R_{-\theta}$?
solution: Every vector returns to its starting point.

practice.problem: Can a shear and a nonuniform stretch generally be exchanged?
practice.hint: Test the vector from the example.

interactiveVisual.caption: Fix shear $S$ and horizontal stretch $D$ by two. Change the input direction and swap their order.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Does shearing first give the same result as stretching first?

learningCheck.question: Which matrix acts first in $(AB)x$?
learningCheck.explanation: First obtain the intermediate vector, then pass it to the left matrix.

teaching.explain: Think of composition as two machines: the input enters the right one, whose output enters the left one.

steps.title: Shear first
steps.observation: Input $(0,1)$ goes first to $(1,1)$, then $(2,1)$.

steps.title: Swap the order
steps.instruction: Keep the direction; stretch before shearing.
steps.observation: The input is initially unchanged, then reaches $(1,1)$.

steps.observation: Both orders send this input to $(2,0)$. Agreement for one input does not imply equal matrices.

lessons.title: Inverses and the invertible matrix theorem
lessons.subtitle: Can every output recover its unique input?
lessons.concept: An invertible square matrix allows each output to recover exactly one input.
lessons.intuition: Collapsing a direction merges different inputs, so the output cannot identify the original input.
objectives: Decide whether a square matrix is invertible
Compute inverses by augmentation or the two-by-two formula

body.title: What does an inverse satisfy?
body.text: $A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I$. This definition uses square matrices. Left and right inverses of rectangular matrices are separate notions.

body.title: How do you calculate an inverse?
body.text: Eliminate in $[A\mid I]$. If the left side becomes $I$, the right side is the inverse. To solve a single system, elimination usually avoids computing an inverse first.

body.title: Which conditions are equivalent?
body.text: For an $n\times n$ matrix, invertibility, a pivot in every column, only the zero homogeneous solution, and a unique solution for every right-hand side are equivalent. Equivalently, every vector has a unique representation using its columns; such a list is called a basis later.

formalDefinition.text: Inverses and the invertible matrix theorem
conditions: The two-by-two formula requires $ad-bc\ne0$. The invertible matrix theorem here applies directly to square matrices.

derivation.text: An inverse forces the homogeneous solution to be zero.
Full-pivot elimination recovers an input for every right-hand side.
The same row operations produce the inverse.

workedExamples.title: A two-by-two inverse
steps: Test $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$: multiplying on either side gives $I$.

workedExamples.title: Collapse prevents inversion
steps: Multiple inputs share the same output.

commonMistakes.claim: Take each entry's reciprocal to find the inverse.
commonMistakes.correction: Verify the inverse using a product equal to the identity.

commonMistakes.claim: An invertible matrix has no zero entries.
commonMistakes.correction: The identity contains zeros and is invertible.

practice.problem: Find the inverse of $\operatorname{diag}(2,4)$.
practice.hint: Undo the scale in each direction.

practice.problem: Is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ invertible?
solution: Row two is twice row one, leaving one pivot missing.

practice.problem: What is the inverse of the product of invertible $A,B$?
Can an $2\times3$ matrix have a two-sided inverse as defined here?
practice.hint: The identity matrices on the two sides have different sizes.
solution: It cannot be both one-to-one and onto between spaces of different dimensions.

choices: Yes, if its entries are large enough
learningCheck.explanation: An inverse cannot recover two different inputs from zero.

teaching.explain: Invertibility requires reaching every output without merging inputs. For square matrices, full pivots guarantee both.

steps.observation: The output is $(2,1)$; an inverse recovers $(1,1)$.

steps.observation: The determinant is minus one. Reversing orientation does not prevent inversion.

lessons.title: LU factorization and repeated solves
lessons.subtitle: Save elimination as a factorization
lessons.concept: LU saves elimination steps so one coefficient matrix can handle multiple right-hand sides.
lessons.intuition: Solve a lower-triangular system to perform elimination, then an upper-triangular system by back substitution, instead of repeating all matrix operations.
objectives: Construct LU with row permutations
Reuse a factorization for new right-hand sides

body.title: What does each factor contain?
body.text: $L$ is lower triangular with unit diagonal and stores elimination multipliers; $U$ is upper triangular.

body.title: When are row swaps needed?
body.text: Unpivoted $A=LU$ needs usable pivots. An invertible matrix generally has $PA=LU$, where $P$ records swaps. Not every invertible matrix has an LU factorization without swaps.

body.title: How do you solve the system?
body.text: Solve $Ly=Pb$, then $Ux=y$. Numerical work must also consider pivot sizes and floating-point errors.

conditions: We solve invertible square systems here. Whenever rows are swapped, permute the right-hand side too.

derivation.text: Elimination turns the original matrix into an upper-triangular one.
Store the reverse elimination steps.
Split one system into two triangular systems.

workedExamples.title: Save the elimination multiplier
steps: Subtract twice row one from row two to obtain $U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

commonMistakes.claim: $L$ stores the negated elimination multipliers.
commonMistakes.correction: The usual convention stores the multipliers being subtracted, without negating them. Multiply to verify the signs.

commonMistakes.claim: Every new right-hand side requires a new LU factorization.
commonMistakes.correction: Reuse the factorization while the coefficient matrix stays fixed.

Given $Ly=(2,5)^T$ and $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, find $y_2$.

practice.problem: Can ordinary elimination without a row swap start on $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$?
solution: Swap rows; the matrix itself remains invertible.

practice.problem: If $PA=LU$, why solve $Ly=Pb$ first?
practice.hint: Multiply both sides of the original equation by the permutation matrix.
practice.answer: The right-hand side must undergo the same swaps.

teaching.explain: LU stores the elimination separately from the current right-hand side. Factor once, then use forward and back substitution.

lessons.title: Vector spaces and subspaces
lessons.subtitle: Closed under addition and scaling
lessons.concept: A subspace is a subset that remains closed under the original addition and scalar multiplication.
lessons.intuition: Lines and planes through the origin support vector operations on their own. Translating them generally breaks closure because sums leave the set.
objectives: Test subspace closure
Recognize counterexamples excluding the origin

body.title: Must vectors be arrows?
body.text: Matrices and polynomials can also be added and scaled. They are vectors when the vector space axioms hold. This book mainly uses finite-dimensional real spaces.

body.title: How do you test a subspace?
body.text: Check that zero belongs, then that every linear combination of two members remains inside. This avoids checking every vector space axiom again.

body.title: Does the zero set count?
body.text: The set containing only zero is a subspace. The empty set is not, since it lacks zero.

formalDefinition.latex: W\le V\iff 0\in W\text{ and }au+bv\in W\quad(u,v\in W;\ a,b\in\mathbb R)
conditions: Use the original space's operations. Do not change them during the test.

derivation.text: Check that zero belongs.
Check every linear combination.
The other axioms are inherited from the original space.
derivation.latex: W\text{ uses the same operations as }V

workedExamples.title: Homogeneous constraints define a subspace
steps: The zero vector satisfies the constraint.
If $u,v$ satisfy the homogeneous equality, so does $au+bv$.
workedExamples.answer: It is a plane through the origin.

workedExamples.problem: Is the point set $x+y=1$ a subspace?
steps: Zero does not satisfy the equation.
Adding two members changes the coordinate sum to $2$.

commonMistakes.claim: Every line is a subspace.
commonMistakes.correction: It must pass through the origin and use the original operations.

commonMistakes.claim: Checking a few sums is enough.
commonMistakes.correction: Closure must hold for every member and scalar.

solution: Zero belongs to the intersection; every linear combination stays in both spaces.

lessons.title: Span and spanning sets
lessons.subtitle: Where can these directions reach?
lessons.concept: The span is the set of all linear combinations of the given vectors.
lessons.intuition: Two nonparallel directions in a plane reach the whole plane. Parallel directions cannot leave one line, regardless of the coefficients.
objectives: Test whether a target lies in a span
Identify redundant generators

body.title: What does a span include?
body.text: Allow all real coefficients, with any signs or sizes. A plotted parallelogram uses bounded coefficients and shows only part of the span.

body.title: How do you test membership?
body.text: Put the vectors in columns and solve $Ac=b$. The target is in their span exactly when the system is consistent.

body.title: Must a spanning set be minimal?
body.text: No. Adding a vector already expressible as a linear combination does not enlarge the space. Remove redundancy to obtain a basis. Dimension will count how many independent directions the space needs.

conditions: Vectors belong to the same space. By convention, the empty list spans the zero subspace.

derivation.text: Zero coefficients give the origin.
Adding two combinations gives another combination.
Any subspace containing the generators contains these combinations.

workedExamples.title: Redundancy adds no space
workedExamples.problem: What does $(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$ span? Does the third vector add a direction?
steps: The first two already generate the plane.
workedExamples.answer: The span is all of $\mathbb R^2$; the third vector is redundant.

commonMistakes.claim: Restricting coefficients to $[0,1]$ gives the span.
commonMistakes.correction: This draws only a bounded part.

commonMistakes.claim: More vectors always give a larger span.
commonMistakes.correction: A new vector may already lie in the old span.

Is the union of two subspaces always a subspace?

lessons.title: Linear independence and redundant directions
lessons.subtitle: Can any direction be removed?
lessons.concept: Independence means that only all-zero coefficients combine the vectors to give zero.
lessons.intuition: A direction expressible using the others is redundant. Equivalently, some coefficients not all zero give a zero combination.
objectives: Test independence with a homogeneous system
Construct a nontrivial dependence relation

body.title: How do you calculate the test?
body.text: Solve $Ac=0$. Only the zero solution means independent columns; a nonzero solution means dependent columns.

body.title: Why is dependence equivalent to redundancy?
body.text: If $\sum c_jv_j=0$ and some $c_i\ne0$, move $v_i$ to the other side and divide by that coefficient.

body.title: Can the number of vectors rule it out?
body.text: More than $n$ vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ are dependent: the homogeneous system has more unknowns than possible pivots.

conditions: Apply the test to the whole list. The empty list is independent; a nonempty list containing zero is dependent.

derivation.text: A nonzero coefficient relation identifies a redundant vector.
Divide by a nonzero coefficient.
Reversing the rearrangement constructs a nonzero homogeneous solution.

workedExamples.title: Find a dependence relation
steps: The coefficients in $2u+3v-w=0$ are not all zero.

commonMistakes.correction: Three planar vectors can be pairwise nonparallel but dependent together.

commonMistakes.claim: Nonzero vectors are automatically independent.
commonMistakes.correction: Nonzero vectors can still satisfy a dependence relation.

lessons.concept: A basis spans the entire space without redundancy, giving unique coordinates.
lessons.intuition: Spanning guarantees reach; independence rules out two different recipes. Both are needed.

Prove uniqueness of basis coordinates

body.title: How do you verify a basis?
body.text: First ensure the vectors belong to the space, then check spanning and independence. Two nonparallel vectors require specifying which space is the target.

body.title: How do you select a basis from generators?
body.text: Put the vectors in columns and eliminate. Choose the pivot columns of the original matrix: they preserve the span and are independent.

body.title: Must a basis be orthonormal?
body.text: No. Oblique vectors of different lengths can form a basis. Orthogonal bases are a particularly convenient later choice.

formalDefinition.latex: B=(v_1,\ldots,v_k)\text{ is a basis}\iff \forall v\in V,\ \exists!c:\ v=\sum_jc_jv_j
conditions: We mainly use finite-dimensional spaces. For an ordered basis, its order determines coordinate order.

derivation.text: Spanning gives existence.
Subtract two possible representations.
Independence forces matching coefficients to agree.

steps: The homogeneous combination forces zero coefficients.

steps: An identically zero polynomial has every coefficient zero.

commonMistakes.correction: It must also span the target space.

commonMistakes.claim: Basis vectors must have length one.

solution: The third is the sum of the first two.

lessons.title: Dimension, extension, and basis size
lessons.subtitle: How many independent coefficients are needed?
lessons.concept: Every basis of a finite-dimensional space has the same size, called its dimension.
lessons.intuition: Different bases can look very different, yet unique representation in the same space needs the same number of independent coefficients.
objectives: Find bases and dimensions of finite-dimensional spaces
Extend independent lists or reduce spanning lists

body.title: How do you calculate dimension?
body.text: Find any basis and count it. For a column space, count pivots. For a subspace, parameterize it and find independent generators.

body.title: Why do bases have equal size?
body.text: The exchange lemma says an independent list cannot exceed a spanning list in length. Apply it in both directions to two bases to get equality.

body.title: How do you extend or reduce a list?
body.text: In finite dimensions, add vectors outside the current span until an independent list becomes a basis. Remove redundant generators until a spanning list becomes a basis.

conditions: These statements require finite dimensions. The zero space has dimension zero. Ambient dimension need not equal subspace dimension.

derivation.text: An independent list cannot be longer than a spanning list.
Exchange the roles of two bases.
The two inequalities force equality.

workedExamples.title: Polynomial degree

steps: The constant term also has an independent coefficient.

commonMistakes.correction: A spatial line still has only one independent direction.

commonMistakes.claim: Polynomials of degree at most two form a two-dimensional space.
commonMistakes.correction: The constant term makes the dimension three.

practice.problem: What dimension has a nondegenerate line through the origin in space?
solution: Every point is a multiple of that vector.

solution: Six matrices with one unit entry each form a basis.

solution: Choose a vector outside their plane.

lessons.subtitle: The vector stays; its description changes
lessons.concept: A change of basis changes a vector's coordinates, not the vector itself.
lessons.intuition: Different road networks can describe the same location. Coordinates are a description, not the location.
objectives: Calculate coordinates in a specified basis

body.title: How do you find coordinates?
body.text: Put basis vectors in columns of $P_B$ and solve $P_B[v]_B=v$. A subspace basis matrix can be rectangular; the basis still guarantees uniqueness.

body.title: How do you change between bases?
body.text: For bases of all of $\mathbb R^n$, use $[v]_C=P_C^{-1}P_B[v]_B$. Recover standard coordinates first, then convert to the new basis.

body.title: How does an operator's matrix change?
body.text: Matrices of one operator in different bases are similar. If $P$ converts new coordinates to old ones, the new matrix is $P^{-1}AP$.

formalDefinition.text: Basis coordinates and change of basis
conditions: When writing inverses, both bases span coordinate spaces of the same full dimension. Identify the input and output coordinate systems of each map.

derivation.text: Convert new coordinates to old ones.
Apply the operator in old coordinates.
Convert the output back to new coordinates.

commonMistakes.claim: Changing coordinates moves the vector.
commonMistakes.correction: The vector stays fixed; the basis and coefficients change.

commonMistakes.claim: Multiply by the same matrix on both sides to change basis.
commonMistakes.correction: Usually one side uses the basis change and the other its inverse.

solution: The two coordinate components swap too.

solution: They can represent the same operator in different bases.

lessons.title: Kernel and null space
lessons.subtitle: Input changes invisible to the output
lessons.concept: The null space contains all input directions that the matrix sends to zero.
lessons.intuition: Inputs with the same output differ by a null-space vector. These indistinguishable directions locate the information loss.
objectives: Find a basis for the null space
Test injectivity using the kernel

body.title: How do you find a basis?
body.text: Eliminate to solve $Ax=0$. Set one free variable to one and the others to zero in turn. The resulting special solutions form a null-space basis.

body.title: Where does the kernel live?
body.text: The kernel of an $m\times n$ matrix belongs to input space $\mathbb R^n$, not the output space.

body.title: How is the kernel related to injectivity?
body.text: A map is one-to-one exactly when its kernel contains only zero. If $Ax=Ay$, then $A(x-y)=0$.

formalDefinition.latex: \ker A=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=0\},\qquad A\text{ is one-to-one}\iff\ker A=\{0\}
conditions: The matrix represents a linear map; its null space is automatically a subspace of the input space.

derivation.text: Subtract equal outputs.
A zero kernel forces equal inputs.
A nonzero kernel vector gives distinct inputs with the same output.

workedExamples.title: Find the kernel from free variables

steps: Different heights produce the same output.
workedExamples.answer: Not one-to-one; the kernel is the vertical axis.

commonMistakes.claim: The null space contains only zero.
commonMistakes.correction: The name describes zero output; inputs may be nonzero.

commonMistakes.claim: Every kernel vector has zero length.
commonMistakes.correction: The output disappears, not the input length.

practice.problem: Find the kernel of $A=(1\ 1)$.
practice.hint: Set the sum of the coordinates to zero.

practice.problem: What nullity does an invertible matrix have?
practice.hint: An invertible map never merges inputs.
solution: The kernel is just zero; its basis is empty.

practice.problem: If $Ax=b$ has two distinct solutions, is the kernel nonzero?
solution: Their nonzero difference belongs to the kernel.

practice.problem: Do row operations change the null space?
practice.hint: Multiply on the left by an invertible elimination matrix.

lessons.title: Column space and row space
lessons.subtitle: Reachable outputs and input measurement directions
lessons.concept: The column space contains reachable outputs. The row space is spanned by the rows viewed as vectors in the input space.
lessons.intuition: The column space asks which right-hand sides can occur. The row space records the input directions used by the output's linear measurements.
objectives: Choose a column-space basis from original pivot columns
Find a row-space basis using nonzero echelon rows

body.title: How do you find a column-space basis?
body.text: Eliminate to locate pivots, then select those columns from the original matrix. Row operations may move the column space, so reduced columns cannot replace the original ones.

body.title: How do you find a row-space basis?
body.text: Nonzero echelon rows form a basis for the original row space. Reversible row operations preserve the row span.

body.title: Why do their dimensions agree?
body.text: Each nonzero echelon row has one pivot column. Both row rank and column rank equal this pivot count.

conditions: For an $m\times n$ matrix, the column space lies in $\mathbb R^m$ and the row space in $\mathbb R^n$. Do not treat them as the same space.

derivation.text: Column combinations are matrix-vector products.
Elimination preserves dependence coefficients among columns.
Choose original pivot columns; nonzero echelon rows are independent.

workedExamples.title: Where the row space lives
workedExamples.problem: Find a row-space basis for the same matrix.
steps: Its two nonzero rows are already independent.

commonMistakes.correction: Even their ambient spaces may differ.

commonMistakes.claim: Row reduction preserves the column space.
commonMistakes.correction: Row operations preserve column dependencies but can move the columns themselves.

solution: No input produces that right-hand side.

practice.hint: The columns are dependent but not all zero.

solution: The span stays unchanged, and distinct leading positions ensure independence.

lessons.title: Rank-nullity, injectivity, and surjectivity
lessons.subtitle: Preserved and lost degrees of freedom
lessons.concept: Input dimension equals the dimension of independent outputs plus the dimension lost completely.
lessons.intuition: Input degrees of freedom either contribute to visible output or lie in the kernel. The theorem counts these parts precisely.
objectives: Apply the rank-nullity relation
Test injectivity and surjectivity separately

body.title: How does the count work?
body.text: For an $m\times n$ matrix of rank $r$, the homogeneous system has $n-r$ free variables, so the kernel dimension is $n-r$.

body.title: What do injectivity and surjectivity require?
body.text: Injectivity needs a pivot in each column: $r=n$. Surjectivity onto the specified $\mathbb R^m$ needs a pivot in each row: $r=m$.

body.title: What restricts rectangular matrices?
body.text: If $n>m$, injectivity is impossible; if $m>n$, the whole output space cannot be reached. Being onto its own image is a different statement.

conditions: The input space is finite-dimensional. State the codomain for surjectivity rather than silently replacing it with the image.

derivation.text: Pivot and free variables account for every unknown.
Homogeneous special solutions are independent and span the kernel.
Original pivot columns generate the image.

workedExamples.title: How large is the kernel?

steps: Input dimension is the column count $6$.
workedExamples.answer: 3; neither injective nor onto the full four-dimensional output space.

workedExamples.title: Injective but not onto
steps: The two columns are independent, so the rank is $2$ and nullity is zero.
Outputs satisfy $z=x+y$ and do not cover all of $\mathbb R^3$.

commonMistakes.correction: It equals input dimension, the column count.

commonMistakes.claim: Injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent for every matrix.
commonMistakes.correction: They are directly equivalent only when finite input and output dimensions agree.

lessons.title: The four fundamental subspaces
lessons.subtitle: Separate decompositions of input and output
lessons.concept: The rows, columns, and two kernels split input and output into complementary orthogonal parts.
lessons.intuition: On the input side, the row space is perpendicular to the kernel. On the output side, the column space is perpendicular to the left null space. These are two pairs, not four spaces on one coordinate plot.
objectives: Identify each space's ambient space and dimension
Test consistency using the left kernel

body.title: What is the left null space?
body.text: Real vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is $u^Tv=\sum_i u_iv_i=0$. The left null space $\ker A^T$ lies in the output space; its members are perpendicular to every column, so they test reachability.

body.title: How do you test a right-hand side?
body.text: $Ax=b$ is consistent exactly when $b$ is perpendicular to every left-null-space vector. Testing one vector is generally insufficient unless it spans the left kernel.

body.title: How do dimensions pair up?
body.text: At rank $r$, row and column spaces both have dimension $r$; right nullity is $n-r$ and left nullity is $m-r$.

conditions: Use the real Euclidean inner product and an $m\times n$ matrix. Existence and uniqueness of orthogonal decompositions will be proved in the orthogonality chapter.
Here $W^\perp$ means all vectors with zero dot product against every member of $W$.

derivation.text: Zero output means zero dot product with each row.
Transpose to obtain the other pair.
Count dimensions using rank-nullity.

lessons.title: Determinants and oriented volume
lessons.subtitle: The signed volume scale
lessons.concept: The determinant's magnitude gives volume scaling; its sign records an orientation reversal.
lessons.intuition: A matrix sends a unit square or cube to a parallelogram or parallelepiped. Collapsing into a lower dimension makes the corresponding area or volume factor zero.
objectives: Calculate area and volume scale factors
Distinguish orientation from geometric size

body.title: How do you calculate in two dimensions?
body.text: Columns $(a,c),(b,d)$ span signed area $ad-bc$. Geometric area is its absolute value, not a signed quantity.

body.title: How do you interpret three dimensions?
body.text: Three columns span a parallelepiped. Swapping columns reverses orientation without changing geometric volume. Coplanar columns give zero volume.

body.title: Does the determinant describe everything?
body.text: No. Different stretches and shears can share a volume factor. Preserving area does not guarantee preserving lengths or angles.

conditions: Determinants are defined for square matrices. Use Euclidean volume of the same dimension; degenerate images have zero volume in that dimension.

derivation.text: Begin with diagonal stretches.
Swapping two directions reverses orientation.
Dependence destroys volume in the original dimension.

workedExamples.title: Area and orientation
workedExamples.problem: What area does $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ produce from the unit square?
steps: The absolute value gives area scaling; the negative sign reverses orientation.

workedExamples.title: Spatial volume
workedExamples.problem: Find the volume scale factor of $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,3,-1)$.
steps: Take the absolute value for geometric volume.

commonMistakes.correction: Area is nonnegative; the sign describes orientation.

commonMistakes.claim: Equal determinants imply equal transformations.
commonMistakes.correction: One number cannot determine an entire matrix.

lessons.title: Determinant rules
lessons.subtitle: Track determinants through elimination
lessons.concept: Row-operation and product rules let you calculate determinants during elimination.
lessons.intuition: Adding a row multiple is a shear and preserves volume. Swapping rows reverses the sign; scaling one row scales the determinant by the same factor.
objectives: Track each row operation's effect
Apply product and transpose formulas

body.title: What do the three row operations do?
body.text: A row swap multiplies by $-1$. Scaling one row by $c$ multiplies the determinant by $c$. Adding another row's multiple leaves it unchanged. Columns obey the same rules.

body.title: What about triangular matrices?
body.text: Upper- and lower-triangular determinants equal the product of diagonal entries. Track swaps and scales during elimination.

body.title: What about products and transposes?
body.text: $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ and $\det A^T=\det A$; generally $\det(A+B)=\det A+\det B$ does not hold.

conditions: The product formula uses two $n\times n$ matrices. Scaling the whole matrix scales every row.

derivation.text: Expand the linear combination in one row.
The additional term has repeated rows, so it is zero.
Reduce to upper-triangular form, accounting for row-swap signs.
derivation.latex: \det A=(-1)^s\prod_i u_{ii}\quad\text{using only row additions and swaps}

workedExamples.title: Eliminate instead of expanding

workedExamples.title: Scale the whole matrix

steps: All three rows scale by three, giving factor $3^3$.

commonMistakes.claim: $\det(cA)=c\det A$ always holds.
commonMistakes.correction: For a square matrix of size $n$, the factor is $c^n$.

commonMistakes.claim: A row swap does not affect the determinant.
commonMistakes.correction: Its magnitude stays fixed, but the sign reverses.

lessons.title: Cofactor expansion and the determinant
lessons.subtitle: Reduce a larger determinant to smaller ones
lessons.concept: Expanding along one row or column recursively reduces a determinant's size.
lessons.intuition: Each entry contributes a smaller determinant with alternating sign. Choosing a row or column with many zeros often shortens the calculation.
objectives: Calculate cofactors correctly
Choose an efficient expansion row or column

body.title: What is a cofactor?
body.text: Delete row $i$ and column $j$ to obtain $M_{ij}$. The cofactor is $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det M_{ij}$.

body.title: How does expansion work?
body.text: Fix one row, multiply each entry by its cofactor, then sum. Expansion down a column works too.

body.title: Should you use this for large matrices?
body.text: It is useful for small or sparse matrices and proofs. Repeated recursive expansion is expensive for large matrices, where factorization is usually preferable.

conditions: Expand along one fixed row or column. A one-by-one determinant is its entry; the zero-by-zero determinant is one by convention.

derivation.text: Group the permutation sum by the chosen column in a fixed row.
Each group leaves a smaller permutation sum.
Add these groups, with no term omitted.

workedExamples.title: Expand along the first row
steps: The second is $-2(0\cdot1-1\cdot2)=4$; the third is zero.

workedExamples.title: Choose a column with zeros
steps: Only the middle entry of column two is nonzero.

commonMistakes.claim: Cofactor signs are always positive.
commonMistakes.correction: Include the checkerboard factor $(-1)^{i+j}$.

commonMistakes.claim: Delete just the entry to obtain the minor.
commonMistakes.correction: Delete its entire row and column.

practice.hint: Only the first entry is nonzero.

lessons.title: Determinants, inverses, and Cramer's rule
lessons.subtitle: A nonzero determinant gives a unique solution
lessons.concept: A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Cramer's rule expresses the unique solution using determinants of replaced columns.
lessons.intuition: If all input directions stay independent, volume does not collapse and the input can be recovered uniquely.
objectives: Connect determinants with invertibility
Apply Cramer's rule under its hypotheses

body.title: Why does nonzero imply invertible?
body.text: Missing a pivot leaves a zero triangular diagonal product. With full pivots, swaps and nonzero scales cannot turn a nonzero determinant into zero.

body.title: How do you write Cramer's rule?
body.text: Replace column $j$ of $A$ with the right-hand side to obtain $A_j(b)$. Use the determinant ratio to find $x_j$.

body.title: When is it inefficient?
body.text: It is useful for theory and small matrices. For large systems, factoring is usually faster than computing separate determinants. A zero determinant forbids division, and a ratio cannot classify all singular cases.

formalDefinition.latex: \det A\ne0\iff A\text{ invertible},\qquad x_j=\frac{\det A_j(b)}{\det A}
conditions: Cramer's rule requires a square matrix with nonzero determinant. Invertibility is also equivalent to zero not being an eigenvalue, as a later chapter explains.

derivation.text: Write the right-hand side as a column combination.
Expand the replaced column using linearity.
Repeated-column terms vanish, leaving only its own term.

workedExamples.title: Solve a two-by-two system
steps: Replacing column one gives determinant $9-8=1$; replacing column two gives $8-6=2$.

workedExamples.title: A zero denominator requires elimination
steps: The system is consistent but has a free variable; division by zero is invalid.
workedExamples.answer: No; describe the full solution set instead.

commonMistakes.claim: A zero determinant always means no solution.
commonMistakes.correction: Infinitely many solutions are also possible; check the right-hand side.

commonMistakes.claim: Small entries make a matrix noninvertible.
commonMistakes.correction: Invertibility depends on independence, not overall scale.

practice.hint: A singular square matrix has a nonzero kernel.
solution: Add a nonzero kernel vector to any solution to get another.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors and eigenspaces
lessons.subtitle: Directions that stay on the same line
lessons.concept: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector whose image is a scalar multiple of itself.
lessons.intuition: A general vector changes direction. An eigendirection only stretches, shrinks, reverses, or disappears when the eigenvalue is zero.
objectives: Verify eigenvectors and eigenvalues
Find the associated eigenspace

body.title: What does an eigenvalue measure?
body.text: In $Av=\lambda v$, $\lambda$ gives signed scaling in that direction. $\lambda=0$ is allowed, but $v=0$ is not an eigenvector.

body.title: What do vectors for one eigenvalue form?
body.text: Include zero and the associated vectors form $\ker(A-\lambda I)$, the eigenspace.

body.title: Does every matrix have real eigenvectors?
body.text: No. A planar rotation generally has no real eigendirection. Allowing complex numbers changes the situation.

conditions: Eigenvalues concern a square map from one finite-dimensional space to itself. Specify whether the scalar field is real or complex.

derivation.text: Move the scalar multiple to the left.
Require a nonzero homogeneous solution.
Find all directions in the eigenspace.

workedExamples.title: A zero eigenvalue
steps: $Av=0$ forces the first component to zero.

commonMistakes.claim: Zero is also an eigenvector.
commonMistakes.correction: Zero satisfies every scaling relation and cannot identify an eigenvalue, so the definition excludes it.

commonMistakes.claim: Eigenvalues must be positive.
commonMistakes.correction: They can be negative, zero, or complex.

practice.problem: When $\operatorname{diag}(2,5)$ acts on $(0,3)$, what is the eigenvalue?
practice.hint: Read the scale in that direction.

practice.problem: Is every nonzero vector an eigenvector of $A=-I$?
practice.hint: Apply the matrix to an arbitrary vector.

practice.problem: Can an invertible $A$ have eigenvalue zero?
practice.hint: A nonzero zero-eigenvector would belong to the kernel.
solution: An invertible matrix has zero kernel.

practice.problem: Does adding two vectors from one eigenspace stay in that eigenspace?
solution: $A(u+v)=\lambda(u+v)$. The result may be zero, which still belongs to the space.

interactiveVisual.caption: $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&c\\c&2\end{pmatrix}$. Blue is the unit input; gold is its output. They are collinear on eigendirections.
interactiveVisual.prediction: At which input angles does the matrix preserve the direction line?

learningCheck.question: May a matrix send an eigenvector to zero?
choices: Only the zero vector is allowed
learningCheck.explanation: The input must be nonzero; the output need not be.

teaching.explain: An eigendirection reduces a multi-coordinate map to scalar multiplication. This simplifies matrix powers and dynamical systems later.

steps.observation: Output length is three in the same direction, giving eigenvalue three.

steps.observation: The matrix is $2I$; every nonzero direction is an eigendirection.

lessons.title: Characteristic polynomials, trace, and determinant
lessons.subtitle: Find scaling values, then directions
lessons.concept: The characteristic polynomial finds all scalar shifts that make a matrix singular.
lessons.intuition: Subtract the same scalar scaling from every direction. When a nonzero direction cancels completely, that scalar is an eigenvalue.
objectives: Calculate characteristic polynomials
Check roots using trace and determinant

body.title: How do you find eigenvalues?
body.text: Solve $\det(\lambda I-A)=0$, then solve $(A-\lambda I)v=0$ for each root. Roots themselves are not eigenvectors.

body.title: What is algebraic multiplicity?
body.text: It is the number of times a root repeats in the characteristic polynomial. It does not directly count independent eigenvectors.

body.title: What does trace reveal?
body.text: Over the complex numbers, counting algebraic multiplicity, eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant. Trace sums only diagonal entries.

conditions: Count eigenvalues over the complex numbers with algebraic multiplicities. Nonreal roots of a real matrix occur in conjugate pairs.

derivation.text: A nonzero eigenvector exists exactly when the shifted matrix is singular.
The first two polynomial coefficients give the sum.
The constant term gives the product.

workedExamples.title: A symmetric two-by-two matrix
workedExamples.answer: The roots are $3,1$, their sum $4$, and product $3$.

workedExamples.title: A triangular matrix
steps: The characteristic matrix is triangular; multiply diagonal entries.
workedExamples.answer: $2$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$, and $-1$ has multiplicity $1$.

commonMistakes.claim: Equal traces imply identical eigenvalues.
commonMistakes.correction: Trace gives only one constraint on their sum.

commonMistakes.claim: A repeated root guarantees that many independent eigenvectors.
commonMistakes.correction: Compute the eigenspace dimension separately.

Find the characteristic polynomial of $\begin{pmatrix}1&9\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
After finding a root, how do you find eigenvectors?

interactiveVisual.prediction: How do eigenvalue sum and product compare with trace and determinant?

learningCheck.explanation: Roots are scalars; vectors require a separate homogeneous solve.

teaching.explain: The characteristic equation finds possible scalings; the homogeneous systems find directions realizing them. Keep these two steps separate.

steps.observation: Output length is three in the same direction, giving eigenvalue three.

lessons.title: Repeated roots and eigenspace dimension
lessons.subtitle: Root count differs from direction count
lessons.concept: A repeated eigenvalue need not provide enough independent eigenvectors.
lessons.intuition: A polynomial counts repeated roots. The eigenspace dimension counts the independent directions actually available.
objectives: Distinguish algebraic and geometric multiplicity
Recognize matrices missing eigendirections

body.title: What is geometric multiplicity?
body.text: Geometric multiplicity is $\dim\ker(A-\lambda I)$. It is at least one and at most the root's algebraic multiplicity.

body.title: Why can directions be missing?
body.text: A shear-type matrix can have identical eigenvalues yet only one eigenline. Elimination reveals this deficit directly.

body.title: What about distinct eigenvalues?
body.text: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent. For a repeated eigenvalue, choose a basis within its eigenspace.

conditions: Discuss multiplicities only for actual eigenvalues, and calculate eigenspaces over the specified field.

derivation.text: Assume a shortest nontrivial dependence relation.
Apply the matrix, then subtract the first eigenvalue times the original relation.
Distinct eigenvalues give a shorter relation, a contradiction.

workedExamples.title: Same roots, different geometry
steps: The kernel of $I_2-I_2=0$ is the plane; $J-I_2$ forces the second component to zero.
workedExamples.answer: Their geometric multiplicities are 2 and 1 respectively.

workedExamples.title: A missing direction
workedExamples.problem: Why does $J$ lack two independent eigenvectors?

commonMistakes.claim: A double root guarantees diagonalizability.
commonMistakes.correction: Check the geometric multiplicity too.

commonMistakes.claim: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues may be collinear.
commonMistakes.correction: One nonzero vector cannot have two different scaling values.

practice.problem: Find the geometric multiplicity of eigenvalue $3$ for $3I_3$.
solution: The eigenspace is the whole three-dimensional space.

practice.problem: How many independent eigenvectors does a three-by-three matrix with three distinct real eigenvalues have?
solution: Choose one eigenvector for each eigenvalue, giving three independent vectors.

practice.problem: Find the eigenspace of $J=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$.

practice.hint: Extend an eigenspace basis and inspect the block-triangular matrix.
solution: The eigenspace dimension contributes that many characteristic-polynomial factors.

learningCheck.explanation: One independent eigendirection is missing.

steps.observation: Algebraic multiplicity two and geometric multiplicity one: not diagonalizable.

lessons.title: Diagonalization and similar matrices
lessons.subtitle: Coordinates that do not mix
lessons.concept: In an eigenvector basis, the matrix is diagonal and scales each coordinate separately.
lessons.intuition: Choosing directions that do not mix separates the matrix action into independent coordinates.
objectives: Construct an eigenvector matrix
Test diagonalizability and calculate matrix powers

body.title: How is the factorization formed?
body.text: Put independent eigenvectors in $S$, and matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$ in the same order. Then $AS=SD$.

body.title: When does it exist?
body.text: A matrix of size $n$ is diagonalizable over a field exactly when it has $n$ independent eigenvectors there. Having $n$ distinct eigenvalues is sufficient but not necessary.

body.title: What does similarity preserve?
body.text: Similar matrices describe the same operator in different coordinates. They share characteristic polynomial, trace, determinant, and rank, but generally not entries or Euclidean length effects.

conditions: The eigenvector matrix $S$ must be invertible, with eigenvector columns matched to diagonal entries. Negative powers also require nonzero eigenvalues.

derivation.text: Apply the matrix column by column.
Multiply on the right by the inverse.
Repeated multiplication cancels adjacent inverse factors.

workedExamples.title: A repeated root can still diagonalize
steps: The standard basis gives three independent eigenvectors, all with eigenvalue $2$.

commonMistakes.claim: Diagonalization just deletes off-diagonal entries.
commonMistakes.correction: That changes the operator; a basis change is required.

commonMistakes.claim: Repeated eigenvalues prevent diagonalization.
commonMistakes.correction: Repetition is harmless if enough independent directions remain.

practice.problem: $D=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)$, $D^3$?
May an eigenvector matrix for diagonalization have dependent columns?
Given $A=SDS^{-1}$, what is $A^0$?
practice.hint: Both zero and nonzero eigenvalues allow the zeroth matrix power.

practice.problem: Must similar matrices have the same singular values?
practice.hint: A basis change need not be orthogonal.
solution: $\begin{pmatrix}1&c\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$ are similar, but a nonorthogonal shear changes length scaling.

interactiveVisual.caption: $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&c\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$, $A=SDS^{-1}$. The columns of $S$ give the two eigendirections.
interactiveVisual.prediction: In the eigenbasis, how do the previously mixed coordinates scale separately?

learningCheck.question: Which condition is necessary and sufficient for diagonalization?
learningCheck.explanation: A diagonalizing basis consists entirely of eigenvectors.

teaching.explain: Diagonalization finds coordinates separating every direction's action, rather than merely cleaning up the matrix's appearance.

lessons.title: Complex eigenvalues and planar rotation
lessons.subtitle: Describe rotation with complex numbers
lessons.concept: A real matrix may lack real eigendirections. Complex numbers extend eigenvalue language to rotation.
lessons.intuition: A rotation moving every real line cannot be described by real scaling alone. Complex multiplication combines scaling and rotation.
objectives: Calculate complex eigenvalues of real matrices
Distinguish real from complex diagonalization

body.title: How do complex operations work?
body.text: $i^2=-1$; conjugation changes $a+bi$ to $a-bi$. Complex vectors still add and scale componentwise, but their inner product uses conjugation.

body.title: Why do eigenvalues of real matrices occur in conjugate pairs?
body.text: Conjugating $Av=\lambda v$ gives $A\bar v=\bar\lambda\bar v$. Thus nonreal eigenvalues pair up.

body.title: Do complex eigenvalues permit real diagonalization?
body.text: No. A real diagonal matrix has real eigenvalues. Distinguish diagonalization over the reals from over the complex numbers; a general complex matrix may still lack enough eigenvectors.

conditions: Rotation angles are in radians. Eigenvalues are nonreal except at integer half-turns. The complex inner product convention is given in the appendix.

derivation.text: Write the two-by-two characteristic polynomial.
Solve the quadratic.
Its complex roots lie on the unit circle.

workedExamples.title: A quarter-turn
workedExamples.problem: Find the eigenvalues and one complex eigenvector of $R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

workedExamples.title: Rotate and enlarge
steps: Their magnitudes mean lengths double at each application.

commonMistakes.correction: Real symmetric matrices guarantee this; general real matrices do not.

commonMistakes.claim: Without real eigenvalues, a transformation is invalid.
commonMistakes.correction: A planar rotation is an ordinary real linear transformation.

practice.hint: Use the definition of complex numbers.

learningCheck.explanation: Conjugating the eigenvalue equation leaves the real matrix unchanged.

lessons.title: Inner products, lengths, and angles
lessons.subtitle: Measure alignment, length, and angle
lessons.concept: The inner product measures alignment and defines length and distance.
lessons.intuition: Aligned components contribute positively, opposed components negatively; perpendicular directions have zero total contribution.
objectives: Calculate inner products, norms, and distances
Check angle-formula hypotheses

body.title: How do you calculate the standard inner product?
body.text: Multiply corresponding real components and sum. Length is $\|x\|=\sqrt{x^Tx}$; distance is the length of the difference vector.

body.title: How do you obtain an angle?
body.text: Nonzero vectors satisfy $\cos\theta=x^Ty/(\|x\|\|y\|)$. This does not define an angle for zero vectors.

body.title: Why do these definitions work?
body.text: A real inner product is linear in each variable, symmetric, and positive definite. An arbitrary bilinear expression need not define length.

conditions: Use the real Euclidean inner product. Both vectors must be nonzero for the angle formula. Proofs of Cauchy-Schwarz and the triangle inequality appear in the appendix.

derivation.text: A nonnegative square provides a bound.
Choose the minimizing scalar along a nonzero direction.
Expand the squared norm of a sum to obtain the triangle inequality.

workedExamples.title: Length and angle
steps: Their dot product is one and lengths are one and $\sqrt2$.

commonMistakes.claim: A zero dot product defines a right angle for the zero vector.
commonMistakes.correction: Zero has zero dot product with every vector, but the angle formula divides by zero.

commonMistakes.claim: Length is additive.
commonMistakes.correction: Usually only an inequality holds; equality requires the same direction.

practice.hint: Take the square root of the sum of squares.

solution: A negative cosine means an angle greater than $\pi/2$.

practice.problem: Is $B(x,y)=x_1y_1-x_2y_2$ a real inner product?

interactiveVisual.prediction: How does the inner product pass through zero as alignment reverses?

learningCheck.question: What must you exclude before calculating an angle with inner products?
learningCheck.explanation: A zero vector has zero length, so the angle formula is undefined.

steps.observation: The dot product is one.
