lessons.title: Vector projection and nearest points
lessons.subtitle: Find the closest vector in a subspace
lessons.concept: Orthogonal projection is the vector in a specified subspace nearest to the target.
lessons.intuition: Split the target into a subspace component and a perpendicular remainder. Movement within the subspace cannot remove that remainder.
objectives: Calculate line and orthonormal-basis projections
Verify the perpendicular residual

body.title: How do you project onto a line?
body.text: Projection along nonzero $u$ is $u(u^Tb)/(u^Tu)$. Its coefficient can be negative; the point need not lie on the drawn positive ray.

body.title: Why is the nearest point unique?
body.text: Any other candidate differs from the projection by a subspace vector, perpendicular to the residual. Pythagoras shows this can only increase distance.

body.title: What if an orthonormal basis is available?
body.text: For orthonormal $q_j$, take dot-product coefficients and sum. This formula cannot be copied directly for an oblique basis.

conditions: The line formula requires $u\ne0$. The latter formula requires the columns of $Q$ to be an orthonormal basis of the target subspace.

derivation.text: Require the remainder to be perpendicular to the direction.
Solve for its coefficient.
Every other candidate adds a nonnegative square.

workedExamples.title: A negative projection
steps: The projection is on the negative horizontal axis; the residual is $(0,2)$.

commonMistakes.claim: Multiply length by cosine and the vector projection is complete.
commonMistakes.correction: A scalar component differs from a vector projection, which includes direction.

commonMistakes.claim: Projection matrices are always invertible.
commonMistakes.correction: Projection onto a proper subspace loses perpendicular directions and is generally singular.

practice.problem: Find the distance from $(2,5)$ to the horizontal axis.
practice.hint: The residual is its vertical component.
solution: The projection is $(2,0)$ and residual length is five.

practice.problem: Project $(1,1)$ onto the span of $(1,-1)$.
solution: A zero dot product gives zero projection.

practice.problem: Does projecting an orthogonal projection again change it?
practice.hint: It already lies in the subspace.

practice.problem: If $Q$ has orthogonal but unnormalized columns, can $QQ^T$ project directly?
practice.hint: Divide each directional contribution by its squared length too.

body.title: What is thin QR?
body.text: A full-column-rank $m\times n$ matrix with $m\ge n$ has $A=QR$, where $Q^TQ=I_n$ and $R$ is invertible upper triangular.

body.title: How are coefficients obtained?
body.text: $R=Q^TA$. Original column $j$ uses no future directions before step $j$, making the lower triangle zero.

body.title: Can a rectangular $Q$ have an inverse?
body.text: $Q^TQ=I$ does not imply $QQ^T=I$; the latter is projection onto the column space. Only square orthogonal matrices satisfy $Q^{-1}=Q^T$.

conditions: The invertible triangular factor in thin QR requires full column rank. A positive diagonal makes the factorization unique. Dependent columns can admit general QR, but this construction cannot normalize zero residuals.

derivation.text: The first original column uses only the first direction.
Later columns use only current and earlier directions.

body.text: The optimal residual $r=b-A\hat x$ is perpendicular to every column, giving $A^T(A\hat x-b)=0$.

body.title: Is the solution unique?
body.text: Optimal output $A\hat x$ is always unique. The optimal input is unique exactly for full column rank. With dependent columns, adding kernel vectors leaves the error unchanged.

body.title: How should it be calculated?
body.text: With full column rank, use QR and solve $R\hat x=Q^Tb$. Forming $A^TA$ directly can amplify conditioning problems and is not always the best numerical method.

conditions: Use the finite-dimensional real Euclidean norm. Writing $(A^TA)^{-1}$ additionally requires full column rank.

body.title: Why are eigenvalues real?
body.text: Temporarily allowing complex eigenvectors, $v^*Av$ is real for a real symmetric matrix and equals $\lambda v^*v$.

body.title: Why are distinct eigenspaces perpendicular?
body.text: Symmetry gives $u^TAv=(Au)^Tv$. Extract the eigenvalues on both sides to show distinct eigenspaces are perpendicular.

body.title: What about repeated roots?
body.text: Choose an orthonormal basis in each eigenspace. The spectral theorem guarantees these spaces cover all dimensions; the appendix outlines a proof.

formalDefinition.text: Real symmetric matrices and the spectral theorem

body.title: How do you find principal axes?
body.text: Use the symmetric spectral decomposition and set old coordinates equal to the orthogonal matrix times new coordinates. Each eigenvalue multiplies one squared coordinate.

body.title: How do you read the shape?

body.title: What is the eigenvalue test?
body.text: A real symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when every eigenvalue is positive. Semidefiniteness allows zero; a negative eigenvalue gives a negative direction.

body.title: Is the determinant alone enough?
body.text: No. It only gives the product of eigenvalues. Sylvester's criterion says a symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when all leading principal minors are positive.

body.title: Can you test semidefiniteness with nonnegative leading minors?
body.text: Not generally. Nonnegativity of all principal minors works, but checking only the upper-left leading minors is insufficient.

conditions: These tests assume symmetry; positive definite here means real symmetric positive definite. Leading principal minors are determinants of successive upper-left submatrices.

body.title: How does the factorization solve systems?
body.text: Solve $Ly=b$, then $L^Tx=y$. The quadratic form becomes $\|L^Tx\|^2$, making positivity explicit.

body.title: How do you calculate an inverse?
body.text: $A^TA$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Its nonnegative eigenvalue square roots are singular values, usually listed in decreasing order.

body.title: Why do they describe length?
body.text: $\|Av\|^2=v^TA^TAv$. If $v$ is a unit eigenvector of $A^TA$, its output length is the square root of the eigenvalue.

body.title: How do they differ from eigenvalues?
body.text: Eigenvalues require a square matrix and preserve a direction line. Singular values allow rectangular matrices and measure length scaling only. A negative eigenvalue reverses direction without producing a negative singular value.

conditions: For real matrices, the number of nonzero singular values equals rank. A rectangular full diagonal factor has $\min(m,n)$ positions; extra input-kernel directions correspond to zero eigenvalues.

body.title: What are the full factor sizes?
body.text: If $A$ is $m\times n$, orthogonal $U$ has size $m\times m$ and $V$ size $n\times n$; $\Sigma$ is a nonnegative rectangular diagonal factor of size $m\times n$.

body.title: How do nonzero directions correspond?
body.text: $Av_i=\sigma_i u_i$. Distinct right singular directions have orthogonal outputs. For zero singular values, do not divide by zero to construct $u_i$; complete an orthonormal output basis instead.

body.title: What is compact SVD?
body.text: Retain just $r$ nonzero singular values to obtain $A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^T$. Singular vectors can vary by signs or repeated-value choices, but singular values are unique.

conditions: Every real matrix has an SVD. For complex matrices, replace transposes by conjugate transposes. Squareness and invertibility are unnecessary.

lessons.title: Pseudoinverses and minimum-norm solutions
lessons.subtitle: Add no undetermined kernel component
lessons.concept: The pseudoinverse selects the shortest input among all least-squares solutions.
lessons.intuition: Lost directions cannot be recovered. The pseudoinverse restores the visible part and sets undetermined kernel components to zero.

body.title: How is it obtained from SVD?
body.text: Invert positive singular values, keep zeros zero, and swap the outer factors: $A^+=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^T$.

body.title: What does it solve?
body.text: $A^+b$ is the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares input. Even for unreachable right-hand sides, minimize residual first, then input length among equally good fits.

body.title: Does it recover the original input?
body.text: $AA^+$ projects onto the output column space; $A^+A$ projects onto the input row space. Outputs cannot recover the original kernel component.

conditions: Use the standard Euclidean norm and never invert zero singular values. Numerical pseudoinverses need small-value thresholds; the exact formula here treats only true zeros as zero.

derivation.text: Split error in orthogonal input and output coordinates.

lessons.concept: Keeping the largest singular values approximates a matrix with fewer directions and gives exact truncation errors.

body.title: How do you truncate?
body.text: $A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i u_i v_i^T$; if $k<r$, its rank is $k$.

body.title: What determines the error?
body.text: Spectral-norm error is the next singular value; squared Frobenius error is the sum of discarded singular-value squares. This is Eckart-Young optimality. The Frobenius norm is the square root of the sum of all squared entries.

body.title: Does optimal mean unique?
body.text: Not always. Repeated singular values at the truncation boundary allow equally good directional choices. Optimality concerns the stated norm and rank constraint, not every application objective.

formalDefinition.text: Truncated SVD and optimal low-rank approximation
conditions: Order singular values decreasingly. Assume $0\le k<r$; retaining at least the rank gives zero error. The derivation proves spectral optimality by dimension counting; the appendix covers Frobenius optimality.

derivation.text: The residual stays diagonal in singular coordinates.
A matrix $B$ of rank at most $k$ has a nonzero kernel vector among the first $k+1$ input directions.
Along that input, any approximation leaves at least the next singular value.

body.title: How is the two-norm condition number defined?
body.text: For an invertible square matrix, $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$. Singular matrices are usually assigned infinity.

body.title: Does a small determinant mean ill-conditioning?
body.text: No. Uniform scaling can make a determinant tiny without changing conditioning. The relative scaling between directions matters.

body.title: Is ill-conditioning the same as an unstable algorithm?
body.text: Ill-conditioning is sensitivity of the problem to data. Instability adds excessive computational error. A stable algorithm cannot recover precision absent from the input.

conditions: This bound perturbs only the right-hand side. Hold invertible $A$ fixed and assume $b$ nonzero. Perturbing matrix coefficients needs additional conditions and bounds.

lessons.subtitle: Transition probabilities and invariant distributions
lessons.concept: A Markov matrix updates a distribution with nonnegative transition probabilities. A steady state is a probability vector with eigenvalue one.

body.title: Which convention does this book use?
body.text: Probability distributions are columns and update by $p_{k+1}=Pp_k$, so $P$ has column sums one. A row-vector convention transposes this; do not mix them.

body.title: How do you find a steady state?
body.text: Solve $(P-I)p_*=0$, then require nonnegative components summing to one. An arbitrary eigenvector is not automatically a probability distribution.

body.title: Must iteration converge?
body.text: No; periodic chains can oscillate. If every matrix entry is strictly positive, a unique steady state attracts every initial distribution. More general cases need irreducibility, aperiodicity, and related hypotheses.

conditions: $P$ is a finite-state column-stochastic matrix and steady states must be nonnegative. The strictly positive convergence result is a cited Perron-Frobenius special case, not proved by finite iteration plots.

derivation.text: Total probability is preserved by updating.

body.title: How do you read long-term behavior?
body.text: For diagonalizable systems, components with $|\lambda|<1$ decay and those with $|\lambda|>1$ grow. Negative eigenvalues alternate signs. A direction absent from the initial state contributes nothing.

body.title: Does unit magnitude guarantee stability?
body.text: No. A defective Jordan block can produce polynomial growth; for example, the off-diagonal entry of $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}^k$ is $k$.

conditions: $k$ is a nonnegative integer. The separated eigendirection formula requires diagonalizability. Finite diagrams do not prove long-term limits.

lessons.subtitle: From edge flows to net node inflows
lessons.concept: An incidence matrix converts directed edge flows into net inflows at nodes.
lessons.intuition: Each edge subtracts flow at its source and adds the same flow at its destination. Total net inflow is therefore zero.

body.title: How is the matrix built?
body.text: Assign each edge an orientation. Its column has $-1$ at the source, $1$ at the destination, and zeros elsewhere. A negative flow means the actual direction is reversed.

body.title: What do the kernels mean?
body.text: $Bf=0$ describes circulating flows conserving every node. $B^Tp=0$ means equal potentials at both ends of each edge, so $p$ is constant on each connected component.

body.title: What is the Laplacian?
body.text: $L=BB^T$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Its quadratic form sums squared differences across adjacent nodes; a connected graph's kernel is spanned by the all-ones vector.

formalDefinition.text: Graphs, incidence matrices, and flow conservation
conditions: Start with a finite undirected graph and choose edge orientations, using the usual convention without self-loops. Each connected component must separately have zero total net inflow.

derivation.text: Each edge column sums to zero.
Thus total net inflow is zero.
Equal neighboring potentials make the square sum zero.

lessons.intuition: Project data onto a line that retains maximal variation and minimizes squared reconstruction error.

body.title: Why subtract the mean first?
body.text: Without centering, a global offset from the origin can appear as dominant variation. PCA axes usually pass through the sample mean; add it back during reconstruction.

body.title: How is the data matrix arranged?
body.text: Samples are rows of $X\in\mathbb R^{N\times d}$, with zero column means. Use population-style covariance $C=X^TX/N$.

body.title: How does SVD enter?
body.text: If $X=U\Sigma V^T$, principal directions are columns of $V$, with variances $\sigma_i^2/N$. Scores are $XV_k$ and reconstruction is $XV_kV_k^T$.

conditions: Center each column first. We divide covariance by $N$; using $N-1$ rescales variances without changing principal directions. Whether differently scaled features should be standardized depends on the modeling objective.

derivation.text: Mean squared projection score is directional variance.
Maximize using the Rayleigh quotient.
Total squared variation minus retained variation gives reconstruction error.

lessons.subtitle: Choose a factorization for the objective
lessons.concept: Decide whether you need an exact solve, an approximate fit, repeated iteration, or compression before choosing a factorization.
lessons.intuition: Writing a matrix equation is only the start. Reachability, uniqueness, and error sensitivity determine the next tool.
objectives: Check dimensions, rank, and consistency first

body.title: What comes first in an exact solve?
body.text: Check size and rank, then consistency. Describe solutions as a particular solution plus kernel. Reuse LU for repeated invertible solves and Cholesky for positive definite systems.

body.title: How do you handle errors?

body.text: Repeated updates of one state favor eigenstructure. Length scaling, rectangular matrices, and compression favor SVD. Familiarity with a formula does not establish its hypotheses.

workedExamples.title: Factor a positive definite system
workedExamples.problem: Which factorization should repeated solves of $\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}x=b$ reuse?
steps: The matrix is real symmetric with positive leading principal minors.
Save $L=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&\sqrt2\end{pmatrix}$ and use two triangular solves for each right-hand side.
workedExamples.answer: Reuse Cholesky; no repeated inverses are needed.

commonMistakes.claim: Always calculate an inverse first.
commonMistakes.correction: Rectangular and singular matrices lack an ordinary inverse, and direct factorization is often preferable.

commonMistakes.claim: A diagram agreeing with a few numbers proves the general result.
